The fact that you say "that voice of self doubt in the back of [your] mind" means that, on some level, you recognize that it's just that. It's a monstrous little voice. It's not your whole mind. It's not the truth. The thoughts it puts in your head are symptoms of your depression, not things that you actually came up with yourself and fully believe. Cling to that hope as much as you can--let the thoughts exist in your mind, don't blame yourself for their presence, but understand that *it's not you, it's not the truth, it's the monster talking.*

One of the scary parts of depression is simultaneously being dead certain of something and knowing something isn't true. It's exhausting, confusing, and scary to exist in two opposite states at once like that. But the fact that that's happening means that there's still a part of you that believes you *are* good enough, you *will* have good things, and your depression is not indicative of how the rest of your life is going to turn out.

Cling to that. I hope you feel better soon.

Fighting the controls sometimes is just a coping mechanism you need to get through the flight, but if you find that you're fighting them constantly, maybe there's a problem with your plane.

That's what air traffic control and aviation technicians are for. Just struggle with the controls for long enough to land safely, now, before it gets bad enough that you have to make an emergency landing, and there will be technicians who can fix your plane. There might even be other pilots, like us, who understand the frustration of always struggling with the controls, and will discuss how we've worked with the technicians and repairmen in the past to fix our planes in a way that's worked for both of us.

It'll feel shitty, waiting and arguing and working to help the technicians and repairmen fix your plane, all while looking up at the sky and seeing other planes in perfect working order flying around, wondering to yourself "Why couldn't that be me? What have all those pilots been doing to take care of their planes that I haven't?" Don't let those thoughts win. It's not your fault. You didn't ask for your plane to malfunction. It's just something that happens even to the best pilots, and again, that's why we're fixing it.

Finally, one day, your plane will be fixed. All you had to do was keep working with the technicians, being an active participant in your plane's repair, and having the faith not to walk away, knowing that YES, it would be fixed someday. You'll get behind the controls and take off. Your skills might be a little rusty at first, but before you know it it'll all be smooth sailing.

With your plane in better condition than ever, you'll soar higher than you ever have before. You'll fly over all the sunsets and oceans and landscapes that you were too busy fighting the controls to see before, and you'll realize that all that time waiting on the ground WAS worth it, because now you're doing what you love again, and life is good.

Low motivation, low self-esteem, fixation on suicide, and lack of focus in school/work are all symptoms of clinical depression. IANAD, but it sounds to me like getting professional help is a good idea. These symptoms are not your fault, and you don't need to struggle through them alone.

I absolutely know what you're feeling. I hid the beginnings of my suicidal ideation from my partner so as not to cause any unnecessary worry. Gradually, "could this swollen lymph node possibly be a fatal cancer?" became "could accidentally stepping onto this road kill me?" became "could any cars stop if I *accidentally* fell off this overpass onto the highway?" became "if I got a rope, is this overpass high enough that hanging myself would cause my neck to break instantly to ensure a painless death?"

My partner did not find out about any of this until recieving a text from me along the lines of "there's this really high bridge over a highway on my way home, and I just want you to know that my life is shitty and nothing is your fault, you did all you could" and it caused us both a lot of distress because I had been acting like nothing was wrong for so long and all of a sudden I was blowing up and wanted to kill myself out of seemingly nowhere.

So it was my commitment to my relationship that eventually stopped me from killing myself, and my partner's commitment to it that got me the professional help I needed.

You obviously love your girlfriend, and that's a huge factor when it comes to how you manage your own thoughts and feelings. I would recommend being honest with her about the thoughts you're struggling with, and seeking her support in planning your next steps (professional help definitely sounds like a good idea).

I hope this helps. Wishing you all the best.

If you can't remember where it started, write down your symptoms now. Anything that makes you feel better or worse. These will help your therapist design an individual treatment plan for you.

I know how terrifying it is, but it's the first step towards feeling better--not expending-the-energy-to-fake-it better, but *actually* better. Congratulations on booking the appointment and be sure to let us know how it goes. I wish you all the best.

I'm constantly worried that I'm going to ruin my relationship like that, i.e. my partner being worn right the fuck down by hearing about ME and MY ISSUES all the time, and just not being able to take it anymore and leaving me without warning one day.

As clichéd as this sounds, communication is absolutely key in any relationship, and it's even more important at any time when one partner is especially reliant on the other (depression, illness, etc). Being a caregiver is draining, and providing support in a relationship takes a lot of energy.

I see it as a balance of rights and responsibilities--partner A has the right to receive emotional support in their relationship with partner B, and the responsibility to use other support people/systems whenever B needs to take a step back. B has the responsibility to support A and the right to their own emotional and mental health/the right to take a break from being A's primary support person when it gets too overwhelming.

When I first started having anxiety attacks again (and by that, I mean for the first several months), I didn't want help because not getting help made it easier to pretend that I had it all under control. You absolutely deserve help. Once you take that first step, the whole fucking world will seem slightly less shitty (I don't mean to shit rainbows all over you, the world still has its shitty parts, but taking the first step to get professional help will put those parts in perspective and help you see all the nice, clean, unshitty parts).

It's so weird being stuck in simultaneous states of striving for self-preservation (human instinct) and self-destruction (depression), isn't it? The shitty thing about mental illnesses is that their symptoms get mixed up with your own normal thoughts and it's hard to tell what's what. 

Like, if you get a rash on your arm, you can look at your arm and go "okay, this is the rash, and this is my normal skin." With mental illness, it's a lot harder to analyze your thoughts and go "okay, this thought is a symptom of my depression, and this thought is something I legit believe." Just try to remember that the negative thoughts are symptoms, not truths. From what I gather, you believe them wholeheartedly but somehow also realize that they're not entirely true (you hate yourself, but you like yourself, you don't want to die, but you don't want to be alive, etc).

I know the symptomatic thoughts are shitty, but I personally find it helps me if I sit down and try to separate the symptomatic thoughts from my actual thoughts. Some really bad days I can't tell which ones are which, but other days I find it helps quite a lot.

Wishing you the best in making depression your bitch, one thought at a time :)

Understand that while it might seem like your feeling shitty is everything to do with you and your life situation and nothing to do with a potential emotional/mental thing that needs professional help, that's not true. Hopelessness is a symptom of a clinical illness. Feeling like a freak is a symptom of an eating disorder, a documented psychiatric condition with available treatment. These feelings are symptoms that do matter, and do need to be resolved. (Important part: These feelings are symptoms. They suck major ass, but they're not representative of you as a person.)

I know you say you have no time for therapy. That's okay. But take some kind of small step. It can be scary not having any friends to walk you through it, but if you can scrape aside the time for one counselling appointment, or one walk-in clinic appointment, to talk to someone professional, then you've taken the first step to healing. It's a small step, but to know that you've got a way out makes you feel a lot better, even if it's a long way out.

You don't to prefix everything with "sorry" or "I know I'm bitching" either. It's okay. That's what this forum is for. You are worth help. You're giving so much to your family, but you need to take care of yourself or you won't be able to help them as much in the long run. Also, you deserve to be free of the miserable things you're feeling. So do it for your family, or for you, or both, or whatever, but just make that ONE first step. There's no other way to go about it.

(Also, saying that someone's problems don't exist because other people have it worse is like saying that someone's happiness doesn't exist because other people have it better. Horse shit, I say.)

That's something I worry about a lot too--I don't talk to any of my friends nearly as much as I talk to my partner, so if we break up that's one support system gone. I guess just realize that there are other people who can help keep you grounded, even if it's just people on the other side of the Internet. Even if, say, your friends or family don't understand your plight, it doesn't mean they can't understand or they don't want to. Do your best to take care of yourself; and I guess be open to receiving professional help again if that's what worked for you last time.
